articles.text: Editor: My husband and I have had multiple near misses from cars speeding up to the stoplight, it is red on their approach. Generally these folks are going upwards of 30mph and they attempt to “slow down” as they have every intent of cruising around the corner without the semblance of a full stop,. When the light is Red in their direction there is a high chance the crosswalk for me, my dogs and the 26 children who live on the cemetery side of Moraga is Green, This morning at about 10:30, a little boy on his brightly colored bike and fluorescent green helmet was waiting with me to cross the street. It turned green and he started into the intersection. A woman driving a white Tesla either didn’t look or couldn’t see past the car to the left of her so she started into the intersection causing said child to swerve as to not hit her car. I have rallied the City of Piedmont and the police department for a No Turn on Red sign for years, but to no avail. We have had so many near misses and we are much more visible than my elementary aged neighbors. Our French grandma used to rap her cane on the hood of cars when drivers encroached into her walking space in Paris. I might start carrying a cane at this rate. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) has announced the August schedule of its “Cop on the Block” program, foot patrols in neighborhoods which began in June. It is the department’s firstever scheduled walking patrol. The following foot patrols are scheduled for August: • Friday, August 4, 12 p.m. – Muir Avenue between Lafayette and La Salle – Office Tyler Petit • Tuesday, August 8, 4 p.m. – Maxwelton Avenue and Nellie Ave. – Officer Jorge Faucher • Saturday, August 19, 9 a.m. – Rose Avenue between Greenbank and Linda – Sgt. George Tucker Described as a way to bring officers out of cars and into neighborhoods, neighbors are invited to bring their questions, comments and concerns to officers as they patrol the city’s blocks on foot at selected locations and times, announced by PPD monthly. Police Captain Chris Monahan, who oversees the program, said, “We rolled out Cop on the Block as a way to encourage more non-enforcement contact with the community. It’s very casual. We plan that each week a member of the department will walk up and down the block for a minimum of half an hour and for as long as people want to chat — about baseball, tree-trimming, parking, crime, anything.” “We plan to keep going with the program until we cover the whole city. Piedmont has about 145 streets and once we cover them all, a block at time,” he added, “we’ll start over again. We currently plan to keep it at one officer a week. So far, the program’s been very well-received; I’ve even had people call me and ask to schedule a time and date for us to visit their block.” Monahan encourages residents interested in bringing Cop on the Block to their street to contact him by phone at 520-3012 or by email at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov. More information on Cop on the Block events, including an interactive map of the blocks may be found on the Police Department’s website, bit.ly/42yYRTu. articles.text: As summer continues, Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping with special summer events or administrative tasks, helping at any of the 66 distribution sites throughout Alameda County. Visit mercybrownbag.org/volunteer to learn more. Piedmont Community Service Crew The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a coed youth-led organization that inspires teens to actively uplift the broader community through service activities. It is the largest of the Venturing Crews of Piedmont Scout Council, with approximately 150 members, It actively seeks high school and older middle school students, and parent volunteers for several ongoing programs. PCSC events and programs include meal preparation for low-income, elderly, and homeless members of the community; home renovation projects, and community engagement work such as youth tutoring. For more information on how to get involved, visit pcservicecrew.org. Alameda County Community Food Bank The Alameda County Community Food Bank needs volunteers to prepare food in the ACCFB Oakland warehouse, and to help distribute food at neighborhood distribution sites throughout the county. For a full list of volunteer needs at local pantries and other organizations, email volunteer@accfd.org, or visit accfb. org/get-involved/volunteer. A calendar of all volunteer opportunities for adults and youth 10 years old and up is available at accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer-calendar. Donations are also welcome. East Bay SPCA The East Bay’s oldest animal welfare organization is always in need of volunteers. Volunteering is a wonderful way to improve the lives of animals in the shelter, and a variety of opportunities are available for all ages. East Bay SPCA’s Humane Education programs are particularly tailored for youth volunteers. Summer service projects can include making dog treats, assisting with shelter laundry, socializing with animals in the SPCA’s care, and more. Participants will learn about responsible pet care, the medical needs of animals, and pet behavior. Other Oakland volunteer opportunities for adults and youth include feline or canine animal care, customer service, shelter care, pet food pantry distribution, event assistance, and animal training class assistance. Visit eastbayspca.org/get-involved/volunteer/become-a-volunteer and learn more. “We don’t have a drawing board anymore, Dude. What do we go back to?”

articles.text: District hires Trevor Meseroll from Berklee College of Music PHS Band Director Andria Mullan has resigned. Andria Mullan, the Director for both the middle and high school instrumental bands, resigned on July 8 prior to relocating to the East Coast. Taking her position in the district’s music program will be Trevor Meseroll, a recent graduate of Berkelee College of Music in Boston. Mullan has taught music in Piedmont since 2005. Her role in the district utilized her extensive set of skills and changed as Piedmont School District changed its music programs. Originally hired as the high school band teacher, she eventually taught 6th, 7th and 8th grade band classes, as well as Symphonic Band and Jazz Band at the high school. She also coordinated a schedule for the PHS Pep Band. Instrumental band directors must have the ability to play many instruments. Directing both middle and high school students required Mullan to guide students with skill levels ranging from beginner to adept. Mullan resigned to be closer to family. The impact comes at a time when the school district grapples with the need to find a replacement for legendary vocal music teacher Joe Piazza, who retired in 2019 after 31 years as anchor of the district’s music department. “It is a big loss; Andria left large shoes to fill,” said Piedmont High School Principal Sukanya Goswami. Goswami explained how difficult it is to find a replacement for Mullan. On July 10, the school district posted a job notice on Edjoin to replace Mullan. After receiving applications, a panel of administrators from the district and both high school and middle school conducted interviews. The district has hired Trevor Meseroll who graduated from the Berklee College of Music in 2022 with a degree in music education. Meseroll is a pianist and educator and will teach the AP Music Theory class left vacant since Piazza’s retirement. He will be in charge of both the high school and middle school band programs. Goswami confirmed that Meseroll will need some support in his first year as he takes on a wide range of responsibilities but expressed confidence in his capacities. Mullan’s departure comes at a time when the school district is already grappling with difficulites in replacing Piazza. His successor, Sid Quinsaat, stopped coming to work in January 2020 and officially resigned in February prior to the COVID pandemic. Erin Igoe, Assistant Principal at Piedmont High School recently confirmed that there will be no a cappella vocal music at the high school this year. Trevor Meseroll will be the new Band Director at PHS and PMS.
articles.title: Andria Mullan resigns as PUSD band director

articles.text: Summer vacation evokes blissful thoughts of time in the sun, bodies of water, games and sports. Conventional theory may hold that summer and math are antigens that do not cross, mix or have any relation, but that does not have to be the case. It need not be a foregone conclusion that summer will be a slow sapping-away of academic knowledge. Even small efforts to keep school skills sharp at the end of summer will pay dividends when class returns shortly. Math doesn’t have to be treated like a four-letter word; parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles and older siblings would be well served to know that fun aspects of math are plentiful during the summer. Math is everywhere, sometimes it just needs to be discovered. Baseball is America’s pastime and a summertime staple, learning about baseball statistics can be a great way to implement an incognito math lesson into summer. In all sports, statistics are a way a player’s success can be measured and stats help us better undertand the game. While watching a baseball game, have your student jot down a players statistical numbers from inning to inning, from at-bat to at-bat. Seeing the change in a player’s batting average can be a very tangible lesson to learn about fractions, and percentages. A pitcher’s earned run average (ERA) changes even more frequently, with every run or Contemplating which of these baseball records is “unbreakable” requires abstract thinking about the game and changes in rules and societal norms. out. Have your student watching a game try to calculate the ERA with every event of the game before they are updated in stadium or on the screen. For more advanced students, baseball is full of obscure statistics like WHIFF, dERA and VORP. Learning how certain statistics are calculated can help understand the game as well. For example the pitcher to start a game can only get credit with the W stat (win) if they pitch at least five innings and leave the game with the lead. Sometimes trying to earn this stat effects the game play, a pitcher’s desire for a personal statistic may negatively affect the entire team. Challenge your student to understand the changes in slugging percentage; which requires calculating the total amount of bases a hitter gets per at bat. Ask follow up questions like who might have a high slugging percentage, but not be a good player? So much of the world around us, even summer fun, has a numerical undertone. The universe can be understood more fully by checking the statistics. This tutor’s advice is to utilize whatever your student is already passionate about and challenge them to deepen their knowledge and understanding with data, number and statistics. A summer infusion of math doesn’t have to come from baseball or from sports. Pedometers can track how far a kid has run in a day, kids bouncing off the walls can be challenged to calculate how many calories they burn or need to eat to keep growing. Tracking height and weight versus time is a fun way to learn to graph and record data. In summer the classroom will look different. Whether on the baseball diamond, in front of the white board or on the black top, math is there and a deeper understand lies waiting for discovery.

articles.text: The popular Piedmont Junior Running Club is back for another school year and is calling all 4th and 5th graders who like to run and have fun doing it, to sign up. Registration opened yesterday, August 1st, through the Piedmont Recreation Department. This after-school sports program is for both boys and girls of all ability levels and provides an introduction to running. During the most recent school year, the program achieved several new milestones, including having a Winter season for the first time. It also had a mini track meet in the Spring for program participants. This Fall, the program is being expanded by two weeks, from September 11 to November 15. Each elementary school will host a Junior program with experienced adult coaches leading the practice sessions. Runners meet on Mondays from 3:15 to 4:30 p.m. and Wednesdays from 2:00 to 3:15 p.m. New runners will receive a t-shirt and be offered a healthy snack after every practice. articles.text: Quite frankly, I still can’t believe I’m here. So far, this year’s Scout National Jamboree at the Summit Bechtel Reserve in West Virginia has been filled with amazing experiences and meetings. From trading glow-inthe-dark patches while talking about favorite constellations, to falling off a skateboard just to get back on, everything has been filled with wonder and excitement. On our very first day I had one goal in mind – to earn a NOVA patch a multi-part STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math) patch earned by completing multiple activities in each area. This NOVA patch is only available at the Summit, as only 500 have ever been made. Because we got to the summit rather early in the morning, we had the whole day to explore the summit before everyone showed up. So, I corralled a group, asked for directions and hiked up to the Summit Center. Once we arrived, I dragged some of my friends over to the booth and started walking around, crossing off requirements. One of the exhibits talked about shaping stones into arrowheads, another put multiple items in liquid nitrogen. When we finally finished the patch, I was incredibly grateful for this group of people – one of whom I had met only 24 hours ago – to stay with me so I could finally earn this patch. Making new friends is a key part of the Jamboree. As we talked to people we met along the way, we began to feel a sense of community, sharing only one thing: our combined love of Scouting. The Summit has one of the largest skate parks in America. Before you even start the sheer amount of safety gear and warnings made me feel anxious. To be completely honest, I hadn’t wanted to come to the skate park. Some of my friends were heading there and I had decided to tag along. Sure, I’ve always wanted to try skateboarding, but it wasn’t something I was extremely enthusiastic about. A large “Jambo 23” sign in a meadow announces the Scout National Jamboree in West Virginia. Diego Branneria (left), Samantha Pell and Amelia Lee (Marin) proudly hold up their NOVA patches. As we walked out into the park, the skateboard felt heavy in my hand, like I wasn’t capable of carrying it. Once out on the large flat of concrete I managed to fall over before even stepping on the board. Fun. After basic instruction we were left with our boards and an enormous skate park. A couple of falls later I was comfortably gliding across the flat… until I fell again. All of these things, as well as everything else I’ve experienced at the summit, share one thing in common. They are all first time, life changing experiences. But they also opened up barriers to new friendships. Halfway through the NOVA patch we talked to a girl from my camp who was interested in earning it. At skateboarding I connected with a girl who kept returning my runaway board. With every new experience, booth visit, or even just chat on the road, we connected. Even if I barely knew most of these people, we shared a combined love and devotion to Scouts. Moving together – and as this year’s Jamboree motto says ­ – forward. Samantha Pell is an eighth grader at Piedmont Middle School and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 1. A large climbing wall forms a backdrop to a cluster of tents at the National Scout Jamboree in West Virginia. Diego Branneria at the archery range The Piedmont-Marin Scout contingent prepares to make flood buckets for communities hit by recent flooding. articles.text: Forward. What exactly do we mean when we say forward? Do we mean trying new, death-defying things? Do we mean attempting a merit badge? Do we mean stepping up to a fellow Scout and complementing their class B? At Jamboree, a gathering of Scouts from throughout the U.S. every four years at the Summit Bechtel Reserve in West Virginia, there are countless ways to follow through with this year’s motto – Forward. One of the coolest things about the Summit are the impressive bronze sculptures scattered throughout and created by sculptor, artist, and songwriter Jamie Lester. Truth be told, I didn’t have high expectations for the new female “ascending eagle” sculpture. Surprisingly, Lester went above and beyond my expectations, creating a gorgeous bronze girl, hoisting a set of wings on her shoulders, torch raised, ready to take flight. While wandering around the tents I stumbled upon Lester, with whom I shared my opinions on his sculptures. Intrigued, I decided to return the next day to attend his sculpture merit badge. The day was hot and still, and I had been rather drowsy all day. But when he started talking, and shaping the clay, I was captivated. Unlike the other speeches and lessons I had attended that day, I kept awake and alert, desperately wanting to see what he would create next. There was something magical about his energy, the way he talked and interacted with the audience. There were about 25 of us crammed in the tent, some on chairs “borrowed” from other exhibits. I’m willing to bet that he touched each and every one of us in ways he didn’t realize. Maybe the Scouts attending his talk and demonstration didn’t even realize it at the time. Something he mentioned multiple times was the importance of connecting with people through art. With his Scouting bronzes, we were able to see ourselves through them, and relate to the energy conveyed through them. It was the same energy I’d been pushing mere days before at the 3D archery targets. It was that same energy that propelled me to try shooting with a shotgun, something I’d never done before. The feeling of shock after the first shot made me want to shoot a hundred more. Shooting has been one of those things that I’ve always wanted to do, something on my bucket list. However, it’s also something I’m morbidly afraid of. My safety instructor, a fun but also firm man, knew of Piedmont. After pointing it out on my shirt, we talked with him for a few minutes about the Bay Area. There was also the man who helped me load my gun when my fingers were fumbling around. All the experiences and memories made during Jamboree will be forever remembered, but it’s the people who will stick with me. The people who made the experiences and adventures memorable were people who helped create and push that energy. That energy that – created by us – will push us forward. Samantha Pell is a member of Piedmont Scout Troop One, and an eighth grader at Piedmont Middle School. articles.text: I am an ADHD Focus Coach located in Piedmont. I work with students and people with ADHD to help them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week I am writing about identifying and utilizing your personal strengths to make life easier and get more done. Strength spotting is the idea that people all have different skills and natural abilities and identifying individual strengths empowers people to utilize what they’re good at to get through difficult times and accomplish big tasks. This is true whether or not an individual has been diagnosed with ADHD. People with ADHD may have unique strengths, such as the ability to see the big picture. I use strengths spotting with my clients to help them understand what tools they already have in their toolbox. One way to identify strengths is to ask people who are closest to you what they think your best qualities are and why. This can provide you with a nice list of things that people around you see and that you might not even see in yourself. Another way to identify your strengths is to keep a journal about times that you succeeded; write down the things that you did well during those times. Then sit down with a coach or a friend to discuss what qualities about you are highlighted in the experiences you jotted down. The third and most popular way is taking a strengths spotting test online such as the Via Character Strengths Survey. They provide a list of common strengths and give you the tools to uncover and understand your results. A few examples of strengths listed are Creativity, Spirituality, Appreciation of Beauty and Excellence, and Love of Learning. Once you have a better sense of your strengths, you can utilize that information to help you get more done in a way that makes sense for you. I work with clients on both understanding what their strengths are and how to use them to overcome challenges. Reach out to me if you are interested in learning more about your strengths and how you can use them to make life easier and get more done. articles.text: Staff Photo Tanya Kononova is stepping into her senior year at Piedmont High after arriving to California as a refugee from Ukraine. Tanya Kononova made a big name for herself as a tennis player at Piedmont High School last year. She won the Western Alameda County Conference’s Player of the Year award after winning the league’s individual tournament’s singles bracket. But her path from Europe to the Highlanders’ tennis team wasn’t a typical journey for foreign students coming to Piedmont. Tanya and her family never envisioned moving to California as a refugee prior to February 24, 2022, the day Russia invaded her native country of Ukraine. She arrived to Piedmont on July 22 that year from Odesa, a city in the south of Ukraine. Kononova arrived to help coach Jim Landes’ tennis clinic a week later, and she instantly impressed him. “It was the week I had the high school girls warm up clinic, one week before tryouts for the team. I told her to come the next day and she showed up to the clinics every day. I knew she was a very good player the first time she hit. It was a good way for her to meet some people,” said Landes. Kononova and her mother, Olga Charugina, packed what they could and drove to the border of Moldova three weeks after the Russian invasion. Her father remains in Ukraine as men under the age of 60 are required to remain and help Ukraine’s war effort. Tanya stayed in Moldova with relatives for two months and waited at the border for 13 hours before passing into the neighboring country. She described the experience of leaving Ukraine. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine, because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova when speaking through a translator. Tanya and her family initially decided to relocate to Bulgaria after a town administration building in Moldova was targeted by Russian artillery. They were there from May through July 2022 and had no connection to anyone in the country. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived with my mother, my grandfather and my grandmother,” said Kononova. “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically took what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week to gather more belongings. She was visiting with a friend near the city center when a rocket struck a nearby building. Speaking through a translator, Kononova detailed the emotions she experienced: “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s when it really hit me. I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were notified to go to a shelter because they detected a missile. Then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions. It was one of the days they bombed one of the many residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night, and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe and some family members are still in Moldova. Tanya and her mother moved into her uncle’s home in Piedmont and have since taken up residence at a separate home in town. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids… I’m still in touch with all of my friends. One of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” Kononova said last year. When entering the U.S. last year, it marked the first time Kononova had an opportunity to play tennis since leaving Ukraine

articles.text: Year-round swim team holding tryouts August 15-17 300 swimmers from seven Bay Area teams competed recently in the three-day Redwood Empire Swim League Championship meet Friday through Sunday, July 21-23, at the Mills College campus in Oakland. The Piedmont Swim Team, a year-round competitive team, won the overall meet by a large margin with 5,045 points over four other teams, defeating Hills Hurricane Swimming in second place with 3,845. Three Piedmont swimmers took home trophies for being the high point winners for their age group: Connor Carnazzo (boys 11-12), Magnolia Stoll (girls 13-14), and Paige Arnold (girls 15 & over). Arnold and Simon Lins before they enter college this fall. Piedmont Swim Team will begin tryouts on August 14 and welcomes all interested youth up to age 18. The year-round team focuses on individual excellence in a team environment. “Our goal is to create a safe and joyful environment for all, one that allows each athlete to excel,” said head coach Stefan Bill. Everyone from ages 6-18 who enjoys being in the water and is interested in learning new and different skills is invited to try out for the team. Swimmers should be able to do freestyle comfortably, with breathing to the side, backstroke comfortably, and have some basic breaststroke knowledge. Tanya and her family never envisioned moving to California as a refugee prior to February 24, 2022, the day Russia invaded her native country of Ukraine. She arrived to Piedmont on July 22 that year from Odesa, a city in the south of Ukraine. Kononova arrived to help coach Jim Landes’ tennis clinic a week later, and she instantly impressed him. “It was the week I had the high school girls warm up clinic, one week before tryouts for the team. I told her to come the next day and she showed up to the clinics every day. I knew she was a very good player the first time she hit. It was a good way for her to meet some people,” said Landes. Kononova and her mother, Olga Charugina, packed what they could and drove to the border of Moldova three weeks after the Russian invasion. Her father remains in Ukraine as men under the age of 60 are required to remain and help Ukraine’s war effort. Tanya stayed in Moldova with relatives for two months and waited at the border for 13 hours before passing into the neighboring country. She described the experience of leaving Ukraine. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine, because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova when speaking through a translator. Tanya and her family initially decided to relocate to Bulgaria after a town administration building in Moldova was targeted by Russian artillery. They were there from May through July 2022 and had no connection to anyone in the country. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived with my mother, my grandfather and my grandmother,” said Kononova. “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically took what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week to gather more belongings. She was visiting with a friend near the city center when a rocket struck a nearby building. Speaking through a translator, Kononova detailed the emotions she experienced: “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s when it really hit me. I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were notified to go to a shelter because they detected a missile. Then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions. It was one of the days they bombed one of the many residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night, and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe and some family members are still in Moldova. Tanya and her mother moved into her uncle’s home in Piedmont and have since taken up residence at a separate home in town. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids… I’m still in touch with all of my friends. One of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” Kononova said last year. articles.text: Photos courtesy of Cyprus Mail Danish rider Jonas Vingegaard won his second consecutive Tour de France. He was greeted at home with a massive celebration in Copenhagen. Its official: Jonas Vingegaard of Denmark has won back-toback Tour de France Yellow Jerseys. He led the general classification standings, finishing ahead of Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar, winner of Le Tour in 2020 and 202. The Dane wore the Yellow Jersey from Stage 6 all the way to Stage 21, the final stage, and finished with a 7 minutes, 29 second advantage. Vingegaard only held a nine second lead on Pogačar through Stage 13, but the Danish rider began tacking on seconds in the stages to follow. He gained one second in the Stage 14 mountains and the stalemate continued though Stage 15’s mountain. But it wasn’t the long courses that made the difference for Vingegaard; the Stage 16 time trial was a catalyst for him. On the brief 22.4 kilometer ride from Passy to Combloux, Vingegaard won the event, adding 1 minute, 38 seconds to his lead over r the Slovenian. Vingegaard car ried the momentum in Stage 17’s mountain ride from Saint-Gervais-lesBains to Courchevel, piling on an insurmountable 5 minutes and 45 seconds on Pogačar. From there, all Vingegaard needed to do was stay consistent. Pogačar found some solace by winning Stage 20, a mountain ride, but there was no change in the general classification. Pogačar wound up winning the Best Young Rider award for the fourth year in a row. Upon Vingegaard’s return to Denmark he was greeted to a massive crowd in Copenhagen celebrating his victory.

articles.text: Singer-songwriter Patti Smith Singer-songwriter Patti Smith will perform the penultimate concert of the Stern Grove Festival on Sunday, August 13. Smith gained popularity with her first studio recording, Horses in 1975, which was inducted into the National Recording Registry at the Library of Congress in 2010 by the National Recording Preservation Board. Her following albums include Radio Ethiopia, Easter, Wave, and Dream of Life, which included “People Have the Power” co-written with her late husband Fred Sonic Smith. Smith is a four-time Grammy nominee and Golden Globe nominee and has skyrocketed on the Billboard charts in the UK and United States for her widely popular song “Because of the Night,” co-written with Bruce Springsteen. She is often referred to as the “punk poet laureate.” The concert will be opened with a performance by Bob Mould, one of the founding members of Minneapolis-based punk band Hüsker Dü. The outdoor amphitheater at Stern Grove is located on the corner of 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. It is recommended to bring blankets or chairs. Stern Grove Festival concerts are free but registration is required. Registration is first come, first served. Visit https:// www.sterngrove.org/86th-concert-season/patti-smith-bobmould to register. Gates open at 12 p.m. and the concert begins at 2 p.m.

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet will perform Starry Nights at Stanford University’s Frost Amphitheatre this week on Thursday and Friday, August 3 and 4. The performances are part of the Stanford Live! Summer Festival. The program includes Violin Concerto, Tchaikovsky Pas de Deux, Blake Works I Pas de Deux, Cinderella Act II Pas de Deux, Swan Lake Act III Pas de Deux and MADCAP; all selections from the company’s 2023 repertoire. The ballet company’s resident choreographer Yuri Possokhov reinvents Igor Stravinsky’s 1931 Violin Concerto in D, originally commissioned and created for San Francisco Ballet’s next@90 festival shown earlier this year. Choreographer William Forsythe’s Blake Works I Pas de Deux features a more modern twist, set to music by young English musician and songwriter James Blake. The production ends with Danielle Rowe’s MADCAP, another hit from the Ballet’s 2023 next@90 festival. The “carnival-inspired” score by Swedish rock artist Par Hägström is paired with Emma Kingsbury’s costumes, and gives the audience a sense of an after-dark carnival. Performances on both nights begin at 7:30 p.m. Gates open at 6:30 p.m. Visit https://live.stanford.edu/calendar/august-2023/ starry-nights to purchase tickets. articles.text: SF JAZZ will host two iconic New Orleans brass band collectives at Miner Auditorium August 17 through 20. The Preservation Hall Jazz Band is a Crescent City favorite founded by tuba player Allan Jaffe in the early 1960s. The band takes its name from the French Quarter art gallery and has been a fixture there for decades, even performing and touring in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina although their studio was destroyed in the storm. They are regular performing guests at New Orleans’ JazzFest, the largest jazz festival in the country. The big brass band is now headed by Jaffe’s son, tuba player Ben Jaffe, and includes singer-instrumentalist Clint Maedgen, trumpeter Brandon Lewis, pianist Kyle Roussel, drummer Walter Harris, and trombonist Ronell Johnson. The August concerts will include a special rare appearance from longtime Preservation Hall Jazz Band member, 91-year-old saxophonist Charlie Gabriel. Tarriona “Tank” Ball, frontwoman of the two-time GRAMMY-nominated group Tank and The Bangas, is also a New Orleans native. She leads the R&B and funk group with guitarist Danny Abel, bassist Jonathan Johnson, saxophonist Etienne Stoufflet, and background vocalist Anjelika “Jelly” Joseph. All concerts begin at 7 p.m. The Thursday, August 18 show will be streamed live. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/summer23/ preservation-hall-jazz-band/ to purchase tickets. articles.text: Visit Filoli House and Garden in Woodside any day this summer to view its many species of roses, the most bountiful blooms of this season. More than 500 rose bushes, representing 150 different varieties, are now in bloom. Horticulturist Rob Joice said that tending to the rose gardens is one of his favorite aspects of working at Filoli. “I really enjoy the many colors, the multitude of smells, and the challenge of working with each rose’s individual needs and making them as healthy as possible,” he said. Filoli has a variety of Hybrid Tea Roses, Floribunda and Grandiflora. Tea Roses have large blooms at the end of long stems and are commonly sold in florist shops. Floribunda are a modern group of garden roses with a wide color range from lavender to apricot. Grandiflora roses grow larger than their counterparts, sometimes reaching as tall as six feet. Also in bloom are sunflowers, zinnias, and dahlias. Visit https://filoli.org to learn more about what’s in bloom and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Filoli rose gardens in full bloom this summer

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now exhibiting Hell: Arts of Asian Underworlds through September. The new exhibition displays how different Asian cultures view the afterlife of the condemned. Hell exhibits over 40 paintings, sculptures, maps, puppets, and religious objects from India, Tibet, China, Korea, Japan, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar, and the Philippines. “There is a presumption that all representations of Hell across Asian cultures are the same or continuous,” said Jeff Durham, Curator of Himalayan Art at the Asian Art Museum. “But in fact, whether they appear in ancient traditions or the work of contemporary artists, depictions of Hell have been extraordinarily diverse: some are terrifying and gruesome, but many are humorCourtesy of Asian Art Museum Detail of Utagawa Yoshifuji, Newly Published Comic Picture of Cats (Shinpan neko no giga), Japan, 1883 ous and playful.” The majority of artworks on view are on loan from other institutions and collections. Pieces owned by the museum are newly acquired and are being shown here for the first time. “This exhibition is like a rollercoaster taking the visitor from excitement to relief; in the end, it shows that Hell is only as bad as we imagine it to be,” Durham said. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/hell-arts-ofasian-underworlds/ to learn more and purchase museum passes.

At 7,350 ft. altitude, the mesa was healthy enough, miles away from traffic, towns, congestion, drugs and booze, a good hour’s drive uphill from Santa Fe. In the words of Richard Colgate of the Long Island toothpaste family, one of the teenaged students boarding there, “It was where East Coast parents sent their unmanageable sons when they couldn’t control them. Horseback riding, stable cleanup, all that.” This was the Wild West escapade that shaped up youths like the Colgate brothers and propelled them, at times reluctantly, toward higher education. One day in the early 1940s, he recalled, a group of well-dressed men in dark overcoats came to check out the spartan campus, their group leaders being introduced as Mr. Smith and Mr. Jones, rather anonymously. “Wait a minute,” Richard thought. He scurried back to his room with its pile of science magazines and leafed through them, quickly unmasking them as J. Soon after, the U.S. government took over the site, shut down the school, and left one rustic building, the Fuller Lodge, still standing today as testament to the early history prior to the super-secret research facility’s launching. articles.text: Family Sanity is sponsoring a solo show by Brian Copeland at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Founded by former Piedmont resident Lisa Scimens, Family Sanity provides resources in mental health for parents of older teens and young adults. To celebrate its 10th anniversary, it is presenting a special performance of Copeland’s show, The Waiting Period at 7 p.m. on Friday, September 8, at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. As a fundraiser for the organization, adult tickets are $50, with older teens admitted at $20. Due to mature content, the show is not appropriate for children and younger teens. For advance tickets, please go to https://bit.ly/3rBLcy3. For more information on Family Sanity, please visit https:// www.familysanity.org. Copeland is an actor, comedian, playwright and author, and a former radio talk show host on KGO in San Francisco. The Waiting Period (Laughter in the Darkness) was winner of the 2015 Theater Bay Area Award for Outstanding Production of a Solo Play. This show is an unrelenting look at a 10-day period in Copeland’s life – the mandatory 10-day waiting period before he could lay his hands on the newly purchased gun with which he planned to take his own life. Even in the midst of severe turmoil. Copeland’s wonderful sense of the comedy of life does Actor and comedian Brian Copeland not desert him (how much should he spend on the gun?). Copeland hopes this very personal, and ultimately redemptive, story will reach people who struggle with depression, as well as their families and loved ones. Interspersed with interviews with others suffering from depression, the play offers an insider’s view. As critic Sam Hurwitt put it in The Idiolect: “It’s a play I’d strongly recommend to anyone who is now or has ever been depressed or who knows someone in that situation. But honestly, it’s such a strong piece that I’d recommend it just as heartily to anyone who’s ever been human.”

I try to imagine what Sally Field thought when she first read the screenplay for Hello, My Name is Doris. I assume she was both moved and excited. She recognized in the role of Doris Miller a character that while eccentric, was also deeply human. And she must have immediately understood that while the story had its comedic moments, there was also a sad, lonely quality to Doris that transcended all of her peculiar idiosyncrasies. This is a film about isolation and regret and a life not fully lived. The movie opens with a funeral. Only a few friends and family members are in attendance. Doris sits alone, grieving; the deceased is her mother, whose profile is barely visible in the coffin. Her brother, Todd (Stephen Root), and his wife Cindy (Wendi McLeadon-Covey) are across the aisle in another pew. Doris has spent her life living with and caring for her mother, sharing a rather funky Long Island house that is filled (or you might say stuffed) with brica-brac. Doris, now in her 60s, works for a New York company that has recently morphed into a hip millennial clothing outfit. She is a holdover, quietly tending to the business’ accounting and data entry, and despite her flea market retro outfits – wide skirts and sweaters and colorful scarves, To most of her young co-workers she remains essentially invisible – seen but not seen. That is until a new co-worker, John Fremont (Max Greenfield), thirty-something, arrives and for a few moments on a crowded elevator sees Doris… really sees her. He smiles and because she’s holding a lamp, reaches up and adjusts her rhinestone cat glasses. And that moment begins a transformation for Doris, one that takes her completely by surprise Sally Field and Max Greenfield in Hello, My Name Is Doris and touches her to the core. She is awakened, consumed by feelings that cause her to all but levitate, as if she had been this loose string on a violin that is now taut and vibrates as she begins to have these Walter Mitty moments where John is concerned. Reality and fantasy begin to merge. Doris has fallen in love. A woman just past middle age, so taken that she begins to cyberstalk John on his Facebook page, convinced that he imagines a Doris of almost 40 years ago and not the person she has become, a woman on the cusp of old age. Doris could easily have become a caricature; however, Field is such a consummate actress that she manages to create a person who while deeply flawed (of course Doris has issues) is not a comic crazy lady in the neighborhood. She is in possession of a wisdom which she reluctantly shares. Adding to Doris’ complexity is the fact that she is a hoarder. Her house is filled with items (old shampoo bottles, lids, one wooden ski, stacks of decades old unread magazines. But her pack rat instincts are not offered up as an insurmountable pathology. Like her mode of dress, she resists the idea that all those years have slipped by. Now she suddenly and painfully realizes that the train has, long ago, left the station and she failed to get on board. She explains as much to John as they sit in a small café and talk. John is clueless about what his presence means to Doris. She had a chance to make a life, to grasp the ring, and she missed it. Now, suddenly, she has convinced herself that she has another chance. Hello, My Name is Doris is a charming and brave character study, carried almost entirely by Field. She is convincing and wonderful as she inhabits completely the persona of Doris. Watching her is a troubling wonder. Hello, My Name is Doris. Directed by Michael Showalter. Starring Sally Field, May Greenfield, Tyne Daly. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

It’s all but impossible to watch The Town and not be reminded of the classic heist movie, Heat, an underrated film when released, starring Al Pacino and Robert De Niro. Hello, My Name is Doris a bravura character study by Sally Field Ben Affleck co-wrote, directed and starred in The Town By Chris Honoré I try to imagine what Sally Field thought when she first read the screenplay for Hello, My Name is Doris. I assume she was both moved and excited. She recognized in the role of Doris Miller a character that while eccentric, was also deeply human. And she must have immediately understood that while the story had its comedic moments, there was also a sad, lonely quality to Doris that transcended all of her peculiar idiosyncrasies. This is a film about isolation and regret and a life not fully lived. The movie opens with a funeral. Only a few friends and family members are in attendance. Doris sits alone, grieving; the deceased is her mother, whose profile is barely visible in the coffin. Her brother, Todd (Stephen Root), and his wife Cindy (Wendi McLeadon-Covey) are across the aisle in another pew. Doris has spent her life living with and caring for her mother, sharing a rather funky Long Island house that is filled (or you might say stuffed) with brica-brac. Doris, now in her 60s, works for a New York company that has recently morphed into a hip millennial clothing outfit. She is a holdover, quietly tending to the business’ accounting and data entry, and despite her flea market retro outfits – wide skirts and sweaters and colorful scarves, To most of her young co-workers she remains essentially invisible – seen but not seen. That is until a new co-worker, John Fremont (Max Greenfield), thirty-something, arrives and for a few moments on a crowded elevator sees Doris… really sees her. He smiles and because she’s holding a lamp, reaches up and adjusts her rhinestone cat glasses. And that moment begins a transformation for Doris, one that takes her completely by surprise Sally Field and Max Greenfield in Hello, My Name Is Doris and touches her to the core. She is awakened, consumed by feelings that cause her to all but levitate, as if she had been this loose string on a violin that is now taut and vibrates as she begins to have these Walter Mitty moments where John is concerned. Reality and fantasy begin to merge. Doris has fallen in love. A woman just past middle age, so taken that she begins to cyberstalk John on his Facebook page, convinced that he imagines a Doris of almost 40 years ago and not the person she has become, a woman on the cusp of old age. Doris could easily have become a caricature; however, Field is such a consummate actress that she manages to create a person who while deeply flawed (of course Doris has issues) is not a comic crazy lady in the neighborhood. She is in possession of a wisdom which she reluctantly shares. Adding to Doris’ complexity is the fact that she is a hoarder. Her house is filled with items (old shampoo bottles, lids, one wooden ski, stacks of decades old unread magazines. But her pack rat instincts are not offered up as an insurmountable pathology. Like her mode of dress, she resists the idea that all those years have slipped by. Now she suddenly and painfully realizes that the train has, long ago, left the station and she failed to get on board. She explains as much to John as they sit in a small café and talk. John is clueless about what his presence means to Doris. She had a chance to make a life, to grasp the ring, and she missed it. Now, suddenly, she has convinced herself that she has another chance. Hello, My Name is Doris is a charming and brave character study, carried almost entirely by Field. She is convincing and wonderful as she inhabits completely the persona of Doris. Watching her is a troubling wonder. Hello, My Name is Doris. Directed by Michael Showalter. Starring Sally Field, May Greenfield, Tyne Daly. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated R. articles.text: In the heart of the Yamhill-Carlton region the WillaKenzie Estate is named for two of the Willamette Valley’s major rivers: the Willamette and McKenzie. The estate began in 1991 when Burgundian Bernard Lacroute and his wife Ronni purchased a cattle farm near the town of Yamhill and began to plant grapes. In 1997 they opened their tasting room and started their wine club becoming one of Willamette Valley’s first direct-to-consumer wine programs. Over the years the wines gained notoriety including being served at several White House state dinners. In 2016 the Lacroutes retired, and the estate was sold to Jackson Family Wines who lovingly shepherd this lovely property. Favorite Wine 2019 WillaKenzie Pinot Noir Terre Basses This is one of the most powerfully concentrated Pinot Noir I have tasted. It could pass for a Cote Rotie from France. Bursting with aromas of raspberries and sweet red fruits mingled with rose petals, orange, exotic spices and a subtle hint of espresso, its’s full-bodied, layered and enveloping with incredible depth at the core, beautifully refined tannins and a long expansive finish.

articles.text: The weather was great and there was another large turnout of 47 walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday, July 26, for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk. An unusual yucca in Piedmont that is visible right now is in front of a home on Hampton Road at Crest Road. It will be in bloom for a short time, so the Wednesday walkers chose it as their destination. The group could then continue on to some of the streets they don’t see very often. The walkers headed off going up Highland Avenue. They decided to have a little variation from their usual route to Wildwood Avenue by continuing down Highland to the little walked, lovely Caperton Avenue and going to Sheridan Avenue. They wanted to check on the new garage that has been under construction at a previously garageless 1906 Albert Farr designed home on Crocker. The group has been monitoring its progress for months and noticed a new, spiral staircase at the back. After their inspection, the walkers went on Hampton Road past Crocker Park (also known to locals as Bear Park due to the Benjamin Bufano sculpture of a mother bear and her two cubs), where they noticed a magnolia tree starting to bloom. After a short walk they came to Crest Road. The walkers were immediately impressed by this unusual blooming tree. Jim Kellogg advised the walkers that it was a chaparral yucca, also known as our Lord’s candle, Spanish bayonet, Quixote yucca, and foothill yucca. A Wikipedia search further revealed that this is a flowering plant native to southwest parts of North America. It has a stemless cluster of long, rigid leaves which end in sharp points of gray-green color. The leaf edges are finely saw-toothed. These trees grow extremely fast, and reach three to ten feet tall, bearing hundreds of bell-shaped white to purplish flowers about an inch in diameter. The fruit is a dry winged capsule, which splits open at maturity to release seeds. The plant usually takes over five years to reach maturity. The group thought the tree was wonderful with its plume of flowers and lizard skinlike bark, which they chose as a backdrop for a group photo. Those who didn’t feel like climbing further returned to the center of town, and the rest of the group continued to Hampton to Inverleith Terrace and Estates Drive, and then down Estates to Selborne Drive. Along the way they enjoyed the view of Oakland, but San Francisco was hidden in haze. At Selborne they went onto Sandringham Road and then a quick side trip on the lovely Marlborough Court culde-sac. In the front of one home there was a forest of beach ball sized and shaped box hedges almost blanketing the yard. Back on Sandringham, the walkers made their way down to Hampton to La Salle Avenue and St. James Drive to see some different streets on the way back to the Community Hall. In all, it was a 3-½ mile walk with some good climbing and lots of interesting vegetation on a beautiful, Piedmont summer morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Patricia Lyons White of Piedmont, California, passed away surrounded by family on Wednesday, July 19, 2023, at age 68, following eight months with pancreatic cancer. Born on April 25, 1955, in Dearborn, Michigan, Patty was the youngest of seven children of Raymond McKenzie Lyons and Dorothy Jean Walsh. Patty demonstrated her sense of independence and adventure early on when in first grade she was told to sit by herself in the hallway for disruptive behavior. Seeing no point in that, she decided to walk home instead. In high school, she earned top grades, served one year as class president, and graduated a semester early. Early graduation allowed her to spend eight months in the Virgin Islands with her mother, who was there recovering from a health condition. Patty went on to attend Michigan State University, again earning top grades, completing her graduation requirements early, and serving (while also having a lot of fun) on the University Events and Entertainment Committee. She spent part of one summer hitchhiking with a couple of friends through the Northern Rockies and did another trip traveling on her own on the Alaska Ferry to visit a friend in Fairbanks. Not long after graduation from college at age 21 she decided one day, ‘I think I’ll move to California’, just to ‘see what the big deal was.’ She packed her bags the next day with no real plan and a check from her Dad to cover one way airfare back to Michigan for when her ‘California dream inevitably fails.’ Patty settled in sunny Santa Barbara right on the beach. Her dad was surprised when he received his check in the mail a few weeks later. For the next 47 years, California was her home. Proving her dad wrong was just icing on the cake. After enjoying her time in Santa Barbara, Patty enrolled at UC Hastings College of Law in San Francisco, working as a bouncer at a local bar to help pay her way. Following graduation, she was hired as an assistant district attorney with the city of San Francisco, where she developed a reputation for her effective court room ferocity. Patty then met the love of her life on a blind date after skeptically agreeing to have dinner with Dan White. Her skepticism was due to her involvement at the time with the prosecution of the infamous SF criminal Dan White. Thinking her friends must be having a laugh, she was pleasantly surprised when she arrived for her date to find not only Dan White was real but he was a perfect match for her. The couple got married in 1982 and were hard to separate for the next 40 years. Dan and Patty moved to Piedmont, California in 1986 where they raised three kids and many Patty White on the first day of school at Beach School with children Mike, Katie, and Brian Former Piedmont Mayor Patty White in her cheerful pink dress at a city function. dogs. Despite her talents as an attorney, Patty left her job so she could focus on her true calling, being a mom. In Piedmont, Patty quickly became a pillar of the community, taking on numerous public service roles. She served as the hearing officer for the Piedmont Minor Offender program, as well as numerous school committees. She was appointed to the Piedmont Planning Commission in 1988, serving as chair for six years. She was then elected to the Piedmont City Council in 1994, serving for eight years, including as Mayor from 1998 to 2000. She also served on the Alameda County Waste Management and Recycling Board for six years as chair. Her friends and family will always remember her wit, charm, and limitless hospitality. Strongwilled and self-assured, Patty often did things her own way with a focus on making the lives of those she touched better. Her rare blend of intelligence, determination, humor, and generosity will be missed. Patty passed away at 6am on Wednesday July 19, 2023, from pancreatic cancer. Dan, Brian, Mike, and Katie took turns staying with her all night, and were able to be with her in the moments before she passed. Our last days together as a family were filled with music, singing, and countless expressions of love. We will miss her and are forever grateful for the time we had with her. Patty is survived by her husband Dan, children Brian and wife Cristina, Mike and Katie, and grandchildren Anthony and Francis White. She is also survived by her sister Holly Connell and brothers Paul and Kelly Lyons. A funeral mass will be held at 11 a.m. on Thursday, August 10, at Corpus Christi Church, 322 St. James Drive at Park Boulevard in Piedmont, followed by a reception at Lake Chalet. articles.text: A stolen BMW without plates entered Piedmont on Oakland Avenue shortly after 2 a.m. on Tuesday July 18. Officers initially could not located the 2020 gray BMW 330, but two hours later the vehicle, being driven by a 16-year-old crashed in Piedmont Park. At approximately 4:00 a.m. a Piedmont officer in the area of Highland & Oakland avenues noticed the stolen BMW speeding on Highland not far from Piedmont Park. As the officer made a U-turn in pursuit, the speeding vehicle crashed in Piedmont Park instead of negotiating the turn in the road by the Exedra. The BMW damaged the grass, a stone retaining wall, and came to rest in a collision with a drinking fountain and park bench. The suspect immediately fled on foot, but another police officer heard the sound of the crash and saw the suspect, a 16-year old, hiding under a bench, where he was detained. He was not injured and was arrested without incident. Police recovered stolen Amazon packages, license plates, burglary tools and knives from the stolen vehicle. Piedmont Fire Department transported the juvenile suspect to Children’s Hospital, where he was medically cleared and later booked into Juvenile Hall. The scene of the crash near the bridge in Piedmont Park. The stolen gray 2020 BMW 330 was found to have stolen Amazon packages in the trunk, burglary tools, stolen license plates, and knives.

One person pointed a black firearm at the victim’s face and demanded he give them his keys and wallet, fearing for his safety the victim handed over the items without a struggle. The two suspects then drove off in the resident’s dark gray 2021 BMW X3. The resident observed a second vehicle, a Lexus IS 300, following behind the BMW. Both vehicles fled up Moraga and towards Highway 13. A short time later, a Piedmont officer located the BMW and the Lexus. Watching Moura’s final shot in the waning seconds trickle across the line past Ajax’s Andre Onana’s dive gave birth to a new a fan thousands of miles away in California, I was jumping and screaming in my apartment like I had been a lifelong follower. In the time since then, discovering the organization’s 140 years of tradition gained my interest. Like college football in America, the majority of European clubs have been around a long, long time and are steeped in traditions. For Tottenham, they were a haven for England’s Jewish population in the 1930s. They became the target of racist chants of other English fan bases, which called Tottenham fans “Yids” or “Yiddos”. In the 1980’s, Hotspur supporters reclaimed the slurs and have used them as a term of endearment ever since. This year, Tottenham took its preseason tour to Bangkok, perfectly lining up with my vacation at the Piedmont . The match was Hotspur squaring off with Leicester City, which recently got relegated from the Premier League to the division below it. The tour marked possibly the final time for Hotspur supporters to watch England’s captain, Harry Kane, in person amidst trade rumors bubbling with German superpower Bayern Munich. However, Tottenham scheduled the match during Thailand’s monsoon season. On Sunday, July 23, rain began to build an hour before kickoff, resulting in a water-logged pitch that prevented balls from bouncing off of the ground – literally sticking like an arrow shot into the grass. The match resulted in a cancelation, but it was a joy to sit with fellow Tottenham supporters and practice all the chants I’ve spent time learning over the years. And for a Hotspur supporter, any time is a good time to talk trash about Arsenal, our North London arch nemesis. Even with the match called off, hundreds of devout Thai fans stayed in the stands to chant the songs they’ve been rehearsing in their homes. Though the match wasn’t played, it was an unforgettable experience to be huddled in a hallway with people from Thailand, South Korea, and England—often answering questions about what made me a Spurs fan willing to come all the way from California. It’s not the pursuit of glory that makes a fan, but the seeking of passion and tradition. And with July 23 being a totally inglorious day, the passion in each Thai Hotspur supporter was unmistakable.
